title: Endpoint variance stabilizer bench notes (microbench)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working note for the "variance stabilizer" experiments. Goal: quantify how a lightweight endpoint-side smoothing layer (a tunable queuing/preemption and prefetch policy) affects latency tail behavior and $/k qps under bursty consumer patterns. Not an official paper — sketchy, experimental, meant to inform a small feature spike.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Stabilizer ON (conservative) reduces p99 by ~18-28% on microburst windows at the cost of 6-9% higher token cost due to slightly increased idle batching.
- Stabilizer ON (aggressive) reduces p99 further (~30-40%) but increases average $/k by ~18-25% in these microbench runs.
- For steady traffic with low variance, stabilizer yields neutral to slightly negative ROI (small cost penalty, negligible latency upside).
- Recommendation: Gate the stabilizer behind a traffic-variance signal (sessionized or tenant-level). Consider a conservative default for hosted endpoints and aggressive for Dedicated where SLOs outweigh unit cost.

Testbed and configuration:
- Models: open-llama-13B-fp16 (baseline), quantized-8bit variant (Q8fast) for a subset.
- Hardware: rtx-a6000-equivalent (48GB) for single-host microbench; A100-40GB baseline cluster for multi-node runs.
- Harness: bench-harness v0.11 (link above), synthetic clients that replay production session traces (sampled 1% of May 2029 traffic, anonymized).
- Traffic shape: microburst windows (10s bursts every 60s) + heavy session stickiness (avg session length 4 turns). Also ran steady Poisson and weekend-like low-load traces.
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (server-side, generation complete), tokens per second, GPU duty-cycle, cost estimate ($/1k queries) using Redwood pricing model (batch amortized + GPU time).

What is the "variance stabilizer"?
- Small module at the endpoint that maintains a very short (100-600ms) adaptive holding window per request class. It can:
  * defer dispatch to allow coalescing into a smaller number of GPU launches,
  * preempt long-running decode slots for short-turn requests under policy,
  * opportunistically prefetch recent KV cache entries for likely next-turn tokens when session affinity detected.
- Three presets used in experiments: off, conservative, aggressive. Conservative uses shorter hold (<=150ms), lighter prefetch, minimal preemption. Aggressive holds up to 600ms and prefetches more aggressively, allowing larger coalescing at expense of request-level start delay.

Representative results (microburst replay, 10s burst / 60s cycle, mixed session lengths):

Table: key numbers (mixed traffic, open-llama-13B-fp16, single-host)

| Mode        | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p99 (ms) | qps (avg) | $ per 1k queries |
|-------------|----------|----------|----------|-----------|------------------|
| OFF         | 82       | 172      | 520      | 280       | $2.15            |
| STAB-CONS   | 90       | 160      | 380      | 254       | $2.29 (+6.5%)    |
| STAB-AGGR   | 110      | 148      | 315      | 220       | $2.61 (+21.4%)   |

Notes: p50 increased slightly with stabilizer because short waits get absorbed into median; p99 drops substantially. qps drop is from extra idle time waiting to coalesce; pricing here folds amortized GPU runtime and a fixed per-launch overhead.

Heatmap (p99 over burst timeline) — ASCII spectrogram sample (time across columns, p99 latency colorized by bucket). Buckets: <200ms (.), 200-350ms (:), 350-500ms (x), >500ms (X). Each column is 2s slice across a 60s cycle (30 columns). Rows: mode.

OFF    : X X X X X X X X X X X X X X X X X X x x : . . . . . . . . .
STAB-C : x x x x x x : : : : : : : : : : . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
STAB-A : : : : : : : : : : : : : : : : : : . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Interpretation: bursts produce sustained >500ms tails in OFF mode for many slices. Stabilizer compresses the tail into a shorter elevated window and pulls mass into the 200-350ms bucket. Aggressive yields few >350ms exposures.

Steady Poisson run (low variance) summary:
- OFF: p99 180ms, $/1k $1.92
- STAB-CONS: p99 175ms, $/1k $1.97 (+2.6%)
- STAB-AGGR: p99 170ms, $/1k $2.20 (+14.6%)
Conclusion: negligible latency improvement but cost penalty remains for aggressive setting. Not worth enabling by default on steady workloads.

Decode-time micro-profiling (sample trace):
- OFF: 60% GPU active time, 40% overhead per-launch (IO/serialization) visible as short spikes; KV cache hit ramp negligible.
- STAB-CONS: 68% GPU active, launch overhead amortized by 1.6x; prefetch hitrate ~12% for sessionized requests.
- STAB-AGGR: 75% GPU active, launch overhead amortized by 2.2x; prefetch hitrate ~20%.

Cost model sensitivity (quick arithmetic):
- Assumptions: GPU cost $X core-min (abstracted into $/1k). Launch overhead dominates for small-turn requests (1-3 tokens). Stabilizer reduces launches but increases inter-request latency by hold window. High-turn sessions benefit less from coalescing — ROI driven by fraction of short-turn traffic.
- Break-even heuristic: If short-turn (<10 token) requests exceed ~38% of traffic in a tenant, STAB-CONS tends to be cost neutral while improving p99. If short-turn > 60% then STAB-AGGR can make sense for SLO-first tenants.

Qualitative observations and gotchas:
- Cold starts + stabilizer: when model instance count is low, holding requests can push more cold starts together making warmup waves; we saw a transient p99 spike on the first burst after scale-up in aggressive mode.
- Prefetch correctness: prefetching KV cache for next-turn can be net-negative for privacy-conscious setups (we only simulated with hashed session ids). Need security review if used for Private deployments.
- Multi-tenant interference: tenant isolation is critical; some tenants with many long-horizon streaming sessions lose throughput when mixed with stabilizer-aggregated short-turn traffic. Consider tenant-level opt-in or autoscaling separation.

Open next steps (experiments to run):
- Run the same sweep on Dedicated cluster topology with strict committed slots: measure whether cost penalty amortizes differently when elastic GPU pricing not present.
- Add real-user-replay for voice interact flows (many short-turns) to quantify multimodal differences.
- Evaluate adaptive hold windows driven by real-time variance signal (replace fixed presets).
- Instrument per-launch energy and power curves (estimate carbon and electrical cost impact of higher sustained GPU duty-cycle in STAB-AGGR).

Actionable recommendations for product:
- Ship STAB-CONS as an opt-in endpoint tuning flag in Redwood API. Default OFF for self-serve; expose as toggle for Dedicated and Private via console.
- Create a cheap variance metric in Console (tenant/session variance percentile) and expose a one-click "stabilize" suggestion when variance > threshold.
- For aggressive mode, require tenant opt-in and a warning about potential unit-cost increase; add an automated rollback rule if $/k rises above X% per day.

Appendix: quick checklist for engineering spike
- [ ] Integration test: guarantee prefetch does not access unrelated sessions.
- [ ] SLO test: run 24h A/B on small set of Dedicated customers with aggressive slow rollouts.
- [ ] Pricing flag: add telemetry tag to measure $/k delta per tenant when enabled.
- [ ] Privacy review and KMS/HSM considerations for prefetch hints.

Notes-to-self: share these numbers tomorrow with Maya/Samir. If we pursue, create RFC that includes toggles, console signals, and safe-fallback policies (prefer fallback to OFF when admission pressure > 80%).

-- Lena
